summary: Sets out the requirements that individual Parallel NFS layout types must meet to work within the pNFS framework from RFC 5661. It separates the requirements for pNFS as a whole from those that apply only to the file layout, which had been blurred together.

eli5.summary: Many kinds of storage can plug into one system, but each needs to follow the same rules. This writes those rules down clearly.

questions: what must a new pnfs layout do

subtitle: The rules every pNFS layout type must meet, separated from the rules that only apply to the original file layout.

tldr.problem: RFC 5661 mixed requirements for pNFS as a whole with requirements for the file layout type, which made it hard for authors to write and judge new layout types.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8434 gathers the requirements from the original layout documents and states what every layout type must address: the control protocol between metadata server and storage devices, fencing, access control and locking.
tldr.outcome: New layout type specifications must show how clients, the metadata server and storage devices meet these requirements. The RFC updates RFC 5661.

today: RFC 8434 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5661, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Layout Types Need Common Rules
sections.content:
In Parallel NFS (pNFS), the layout type decides how a client reads and writes data on storage devices. Layout types can differ in how I/O is done, what the metadata server (MDS) and storage devices must tell each other, how the system ensures I/O is only processed when the client holds a layout, and how opaque data fields are interpreted.

The file layout was defined in RFC 5661. The block layout was defined in RFC 5663, the object layout in RFC 5664, and the SCSI layout later in RFC 8154. Because the file layout lived inside the main NFSv4.1 document, some implementers read Sections 12 and 13 of that document as applying only to the file layout. Authors of new layout types then struggled to tell what they had to meet.

This document gathers the requirements from the original Standards Track documents and states those placed on all layout types, whatever type they choose.
sections.eli5: Some builders thought the building rules only applied to the first kind of building. This document says which rules apply to every building.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
The RFC defines terms that the rest of the document relies on.

  • Layout: the information a client uses to access file data on a storage device, including the layout type and which storage devices to use.
  • Layout type: the storage protocol used to reach the data plus the aggregation scheme used to lay file data out across storage devices.
  • Control protocol: whatever mechanism an implementation uses to meet the control communication requirement. It need not be a protocol as normally understood.
  • Storage protocol: what clients use to do I/O to the storage device.
  • Fencing: the metadata server preventing storage devices from processing I/O from a specific client to a specific file.
  • Recalling vs. revoking: a recall is graceful, so the client can flush writes first. A revocation invalidates the layout, and storage devices will no longer accept access based on it.

The RFC prefers the general term storage device over data server. Every data server is a storage device, but a device that uses a non-file protocol is not a data server. One device can act as a data server for some layout types and a plain storage device for others.

It also notes that it differs from most Standards Track documents: it sets requirements for those who define layout types, and it says which requirements apply to implementations.
sections.eli5: Before the rules, there is a word list so everyone means the same thing. For example, 'fencing' means putting up a fence so one visitor cannot touch a particular file.

sections.title: The Control Protocol Models
sections.content:
A layout type must meet requirements on how the metadata server and storage devices interact, so that clients see a consistent view of stored data and locking state. Implementations may satisfy them in any manner, and the specification must clearly show how.

The RFC describes the ways this can work.

  • Loose coupling: there is no control protocol other than the storage protocol, so the metadata server, storage devices and client may change independently. The block and object layouts use this model.
  • Purpose-built control protocol: the metadata and data servers are designed as a unit, and interoperability must hold between clients and each metadata-data server pair. The file layout uses this model.
  • Standards Track control protocol: either a new layout type defines an obligatory one, or a separate document defines one that meets the requirements of an existing layout type.

The SCSI layout is an example of the last case. It extends the block layout, which required fencing but gave the control protocol no way to fence the client. The SCSI layout remedies that and in effect has a tightly coupled model. The RFC calls a design tightly coupled when the control protocol is one designed specifically for control communication.
sections.eli5: There are different ways for the front desk and the warehouse to talk. They might just use the same phone line as customers, or they might have a private hotline.

sections.title: The Requirements on Every Layout Type
sections.content:
Section 3.1 lists five requirements for interactions between the metadata server and storage devices.

  1. The metadata server MUST be able to service a client's I/O if the client sends it to the metadata server instead of the storage device, even after granting a layout.
  2. The metadata server MUST be able to restrict access to a file on the storage devices when it revokes a layout. No such requirement applies to a mere recall. It applies only once the server decides the client is not returning the layout gracefully.
  3. A pNFS implementation MUST NOT allow violation of NFSv4.1 access controls: ACLs and file open modes.
  4. Interactions between locking and I/O MUST obey existing semantic restrictions. If an I/O would be invalid at the metadata server, it must not be allowed at the storage device. For block and SCSI layouts the client must enforce this.
  5. Any disagreement between metadata server and data server about attributes such as modify time, change attribute and EOF position MUST be of limited duration, with clear means of resolution.

Different layout types may satisfy these differently. The file layout, for example, uses the stateid to fence off the client. Each new layout type document MUST address how the client, metadata server and storage devices interact to meet the requirements.
sections.eli5: The rules say the front desk must always be able to help, must be able to cut a visitor off, and must never let anyone break the file's privacy rules.

sections.title: Unwritten Rules and Editorial Duties
sections.content:
Section 3.2 spells out requirements that existing layout types already followed but RFC 5661 did not state. Clients MUST NOT do I/O to a storage device without a layout for the file, MUST NOT do I/O outside the byte ranges in the layout segment, and MUST NOT do I/O inconsistent with the layout iomode.

With the file layout, storage devices can reject requests that break these rules. Other layout types may not be able to, which puts the burden on the client. For those types, the metadata server MAY use fencing operations to enforce revocation. It MUST allow clients to perform data I/O against it even if it has granted a layout. A layout type might discourage that I/O but cannot forbid it. And the metadata server MUST be able to do storage allocation: creating, deleting, extending or truncating files.

Section 3.3 covers how to write a layout type document. It must make clear how the client, metadata server and storage device act together to meet the requirements. The RFC states that if a document does not impose requirements sufficient to ensure the semantic requirements are met, it is not appropriate for publication as an RFC from the IETF stream.
sections.eli5: Some rules were never written down even though everyone followed them, like staying inside the lines you were given. Now they are written down, and any new warehouse design that skips them cannot be approved.

sections.title: How the Original Layout Types Compare
sections.content:
Section 4 is not normative for the original layout types. It shows how each one meets the requirements, to explain the updates made to Section 12 of RFC 5661.

The file layout comes closest to ordinary NFSv4.1 semantics. The stateid and principal used for I/O must have the same effect, and be validated the same way, on a data server as on the metadata server. Storage devices can also fence an I/O when the metadata server has rejected the stateid. The client should treat NFS4ERR_BAD_STATEID as meaning it has been fenced from the file and should contact the metadata server.

With the block layout, storage devices generally cannot enforce file-based security. SAN access control works on whole disks and whole hosts. The burden shifts to the client, and fencing happens at the level of the host and logical unit, so one revocation can effectively revoke all of a client's layouts on that logical volume.

With the object layout, security checks happen when the layout is allocated. The layout carries object capabilities. The metadata server MUST change the capability version attribute to invalidate outstanding capabilities when permissions change, a conflicting mandatory byte-range lock is granted, or a layout is revoked and reassigned.
sections.eli5: The three early designs put the guard in different places. The file design lets the warehouse check each visitor, the block design trusts the visitor to follow the rules, and the object design gives the visitor a pass that can be cancelled.

sections.title: Summary and Security
sections.content:
In the three original layout types, the burden of enforcing NFSv4.1 security can fall to the storage devices (files), the client (blocks) or the metadata server (objects). New layout type documents MUST address the fencing of clients after a layout is revoked, and the security implications of the storage devices' native capabilities against the NFSv4.1 security model. They also need to show how other requirements, such as locking, are met.

The security section gives a framework rather than rules for particular layouts. The layout type specification must ensure only data access consistent with the NFSv4.1 security model is allowed, either by checks at each access or by making the client or storage device responsible. In the latter case, access rights are reflected in layouts, and the layout type must prevent inappropriate access caused by permission changes after a layout is granted. The metadata server MUST be able to fence a client from the data file, and revocation MUST end the client's access at the storage devices. The client can then reacquire the layout and be checked against current permissions. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If a visitor is told to leave, the fence has to really stop them. They can come back later and be checked again under the new rules.
